content: Professor Skeaff is a member of the Public Health Scientific Advisory Group of the New Zealand National Heart Foundation. This group provides scientific advice to the Heart Foundation, a non-governmental organization, to support its public health initiatives aimed at reducing the burden of heart disease in New Zealand. Professor Skeaff is not an employee of the Heart Foundation and does not receive any remuneration for his work with the Advisory Group, a role he has held since 2004. He also serves as the Chair of the Food and Nutrition Working Group of the New Zealand National Heart Foundation. This group advises the Foundation on its food and nutrition programs to combat heart disease in New Zealand. Similar to his other role, he is not an employee of the Foundation and does not receive payment for his contributions to the Working Group, a position he has held since 2004. In 2008, Professor Skeaff was appointed as a Scientific Fellow of Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ). This network fosters collaboration between FSANZ staff, Fellows, and their affiliated institutions for mutual benefit. Fellows do not receive financial compensation for their involvement. Professor Skeaff is also a member of the New Zealand Food Safety Academy (NZFSA), a government department within the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. The NZFSA occasionally seeks advice from its expert members in areas where its staff lacks expertise or to validate staff recommendations. Additionally, the NZFSA forms expert groups to address specific issues, drawing on the expertise of Academy members. Professor Skeaff has been involved with the NZFSA since 2008. He has also been a member of the New Zealand Nutrition Foundation Scientific Advisory Committee, which provides independent scientific opinions on the Foundation's work. Although the committee has not convened or sought member input since 2005–2006, his name remains listed on the Foundation's website as a member of the Advisory Group. It was determined that his declared interests do not pose any conflict of interest for his role in the WHO Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG) Subgroup on Diet and Health, nor for the work being conducted by this subgroup. Professor Vorster disclosed her role on the Scientific Panel advising the South African Sugar Association (SASA) on nutrition research funding for South African universities. She emphasized that her participation does not obligate her to support SASA's policies or viewpoints, and she has not received any financial benefits from SASA. However, SASA promotes the global competitiveness, profitability, and sustainability of the South African sugar industry. It was suggested that Professor Vorster could continue serving on the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health but should abstain from discussions and decisions related to free sugars recommendations. She may fully participate in discussions on other topics, such as fats and fatty acids. External resource persons, who are experts invited to NUGAG meetings for specific tasks, contributed to evidence reviews but did not vote on recommendations. Their declared interests were recorded for transparency but were not assessed for conflicts of interest, as they did not influence the final recommendations. Several external resource persons and peer reviewers declared no conflicts of interest. Others disclosed their involvement in various research projects, advisory roles, or expert testimonies, often without financial compensation or with funds directed to their research institutions. For example, Professor Ingeborg Brouwer assisted in preparing an expert witness report on conjugated linoleic acids but declined financial compensation. Professor Francesco Cappuccio provided expert testimony on salt and cardiovascular disease and is an unpaid member of several salt-related health organizations. Professor Russell de Souza disclosed involvement in a research grant funded by Coca-Cola, which supported systematic reviews on fructose and cardiovascular disease risk. Professor Ronald Mensink declared research funding from various organizations, with funds directed to his research unit, NUTRIM. The WHO guidelines on sugar intake for adults and children were informed by systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and expert consultations. These guidelines aim to address the global burden of non-communicable diseases, including dental caries, obesity, and cardiovascular diseases, by providing evidence-based recommendations on dietary sugar consumption.
